Plainim

Game StrategyPlace Value
Game: Take turns changing chips on one row of the board. Whoever takes the last chip wins.
How to play: Click squares in a single row to mark chips to remove or empty squares to fill (only to the right of a chip you remove). Then press Make move.

Look for the math

Plainim looks like a board game with chips, but each row is really a number written in binary. Once you see that, the winning plan is the same secret that runs through every form of Nim.

Rows are heaps, columns are bits

Read a row from left to right as a binary number: the leftmost column is the highest place value. A chip means 1, an empty square means 0. So a row of five cells with chips only in the first and last squares is the number 10001 in binary — seventeen in ordinary counting. The numbers under the board are those place values.

Every legal move lowers a heap

The rules force your leftmost mark to remove a chip. That means the highest bit you change always goes from 1 to 0, so the row’s number always gets smaller. You may flip any bits to its right — adding or removing — and that is exactly choosing any smaller non-negative value for that heap. The logic test checks every legal mask on boards up to six columns: each one strictly lowers its heap.

Balance the binary digits

XOR every row’s number together. That combined value is the Nim-sum. If it is already zero, every move leaves a non-zero sum and a careful opponent can always answer. If it is not zero, there is a move that makes it zero — change one row so that, bit by bit, every column has an even number of chips across the whole board. The page’s tip is the same advice: after your move, only matched digits should be left over.

Misère is almost the same

With Misère checked, the player who takes the last chip loses. The usual Nim-sum plan still works until every heap has size at most one, with at most one bigger heap left — then the applet’s endgame kicks in and leaves that big heap as 0 or 1 so you are the one stuck with the last chip.

Turn on a small board (3 columns, 2 rows) and after every move check whether each column has an even number of chips. When you can keep that true, the computer is the one who faces the empty board.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
